stem: A child with autism spectrum disorder becomes distressed by unexpected procedures. The child needs a blood draw that was not part of the usual routine. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Before the blood draw, give a brief clear explanation and use a visual schedule or Social Story to show the sequence of what to expect, keeping the process as predictable as possible.
options.B: Begin the blood draw without advance visual preparation and explain each step only after it occurs so the change in routine is not emphasized beforehand.
options.C: Prepare a visual schedule, but deliberately change the sequence during the procedure so the child practices tolerating unexpected transitions.
options.D: Use verbal instructions alone and withhold the child's usual visual supports because medical procedures should be managed differently from other unfamiliar activities.

rationale: Current guidance supports adapting care for autistic children with meaningful visual supports and greater predictability. CDC describes autism-focused educational approaches that use consistency, written or drawn routines, visual instructions, and Social Stories that give simple descriptions of what to expect. NICE recommends visual supports in health and social care and identifies absence of predictability and structure as a factor that can contribute to behavior that challenges. Therefore A best fits this child, who is specifically distressed by an unexpected procedure. B withholds advance structure, C intentionally makes the sequence unpredictable, and D removes visual supports rather than adapting communication to the child's needs.
educational_objective: Prepare an autistic child for an unfamiliar procedure using individualized, clear visual supports and a predictable sequence rather than introducing avoidable unexpected changes.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
source_document_title: Treatment and Intervention for Autism Spectrum Disorder; Autism spectrum disorder in under 19s: support and management (CG170)
source_version_date: CDC page dated May 16, 2024 and live accessed 2026-08-16; NICE CG170 last updated June 14, 2021 and last reviewed September 5, 2025, current as accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: CDC > Types of Treatments > Educational approaches (TEACCH: consistency, written/drawn routines, visual instructions) and Social-relational approaches (Social Stories: simple descriptions of what to expect). NICE CG170 > 1.1.9 Making adjustments to the social and physical environment and processes of care (meaningful visual supports) and 1.4.1 Anticipating and preventing behaviour that challenges (changes to routines; absence of predictability and structure).
source_claim_supported: For autistic children, care can be adapted with consistency and visual supports; written/drawn routines and Social Stories can provide information about what to expect, while health-care guidance recommends meaningful visual supports and recognizes lack of predictability/structure as a potential contributor to challenging behavior.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity, page 10: provide appropriate care for a client experiencing visual, auditory and/or cognitive alterations; use therapeutic communication techniques; incorporate behavioral management techniques when caring for a client.
blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — individualized communication and behavioral support during care

source_original.stem: A child with autism spectrum disorder becomes distressed by unexpected procedures. The child needs a blood draw that was not part of the usual routine. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Give a simple advance explanation and use a visual schedule or social story to show what will happen, preserving predictability before care begins today.
options.B: Give a detailed verbal explanation after the procedure begins because advance preparation may increase distress when the child's routine is changing.
options.C: Use figurative language and indirect hints before the procedure because abstract communication promotes flexibility more effectively than concrete information.
options.D: Change the care routine frequently without advance explanation because repeated unexpected changes are the preferred way to reduce distress over time.

source_original.rationale: Predictability and concrete preparation can reduce distress for many children with autism. Option A is correct because CDC describes consistency, visual supports, and Social Stories that give simple descriptions of what to expect. Option B delays preparation until after the procedure begins. Option C relies on abstract figurative language rather than concrete information. Option D deliberately increases unexpected change rather than predictability.
source_original.source_detail: CDC — Treatment and Intervention for Autism Spectrum Disorder, developmental/educational supports: many autistic people benefit from consistency, routines that can be written or drawn, pairing verbal instructions with visual supports, and Social Stories that provide simple descriptions of what to expect in a situation. Current CDC autism treatment/intervention guidance live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Psychosocial Integrity: mental-health symptom recognition, therapeutic communication, behavioral adaptation and culturally/person-centered psychosocial support as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the stem, construct and key A. Added current NICE health-care-specific guidance to close the source-to-clinical-setting gap, removed unsupported claims that predictability necessarily reduces distress, and rewrote distractors so each conflicts with supported visual-support/predictability principles without fabricated mechanisms.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Communication and procedural preparation for an autistic child
audit_findings.source_authority: Current CDC autism treatment guidance plus current NICE autism support/management guideline; NCSBN for blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: CDC page dated 2024 and live-rechecked 2026-08-16; NICE guideline last reviewed 2025 and retained as current
audit_findings.exact_locator: CDC Educational approaches/TEACCH and Social-relational approaches/Social Stories; NICE 1.1.9 and 1.4.1; NCSBN Psychosocial Integrity page 10
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final answer uses only supported principles: meaningful visual supports, consistency/predictability, written/drawn routines, and simple information about what to expect. No unverified claim about guaranteed anxiety/distress reduction, timing duration, or behavioral mechanism remains.

distractor_audit.A: Applies visual support and predictability to the unexpected procedure and is fully aligned with the cited guidance.
distractor_audit.B: Withholds advance visual structure despite the child's known difficulty with unexpected procedures.
distractor_audit.C: Adds deliberate unpredictability, conflicting with consistency and the identified risk from absence of predictability/structure.
distractor_audit.D: Removes visual supports rather than making the recommended care-process adjustment.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A provides the supported adaptation without simultaneously removing or undermining predictability/visual support.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe concrete procedural-preparation strategies; the correct choice is not signaled by terminology alone.
audit_findings.blueprint: Psychosocial Integrity — therapeutic communication, behavioral support and care adapted to cognitive alterations.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the blood-draw application against CDC and health-care-specific NICE guidance, each option, rationale, objective, NCSBN category, cueing and second-answer risk from zero; A remained uniquely best.
